extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and practitioners studying English common law
extracted.subtask_short: law of master and servant and marriage
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of English common-law principles governing the military and maritime states, master-and-servant relations, and the law of marriage (formation, impediments, and civil consequences). Draws on statutes, precedent, and comparative civil/canon law reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks of servitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Servitude is characterized where the law is concealed or precarious ('misera est servitus, ubi jus est vagum aut incognitum').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hidden or uncertain legal rights foster a state of servitude and social envy; free states should guard against institutional arrangements that create such invidious distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautions against armed slaves/soldiery as servitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Free governments should either prevent the introduction of slavery entirely, or if slavery exists, not entrust slaves with arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing an armed enslaved class creates a danger to the free population; soldiers should not form a distinct servile order within the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory relief and privileges for soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (e.g., 43 Eliz. c. 3.) weekly allowances for sick, hurt, and maimed soldiers; royal hospitals (Chelsea); post-service freedoms to use trades; ability to make informal wills while in actual military service (various statutes cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament has enacted statutes to provide for soldiers' relief, reintegration into civilian occupations, and simplified testamentary acts in service—these are humane exceptions to ordinary legal formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval/maritime constitutional importance and historic laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The royal navy is the island's chief defence; maritime law traditions (e.g., Laws of Oleron) and historical statutes are foundational to marine constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical sources and navigation statutes shaped England's maritime supremacy; statutory regulation (including master/mariners composition rules) has been used to build naval capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigation Acts and mercantile regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Navigation acts (origins 1650 onward, continued at Restoration) limited trade to English bottoms and favored English shipping and crews (e.g., master and three-fourths of mariners to be English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutes were designed to encourage English shipping and commerce, sometimes with political/strategic motives; they shaped trade and nationality requirements for vessels and crews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of supplying the navy: impressment and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Impressment by the crown's commission has ancient precedent and is treated as part of the common law; other methods include parish binding of apprentices (protected for first three years), volunteer inducements, and naturalization of foreign seamen after service. A registry scheme was proposed and later abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impressment is defensible only by public necessity; statutes and local procedures limit or modify the practice and provide protections (e.g., exemptions for fishermen, penalties for hiding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval discipline regulated by parliamentary articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles, orders and rules enacted by Parliament (post-Restoration and revised later) enumerate offences and punishments for seamen; naval regulation differs from the army where articles were historically at the crown's pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary enactment of naval articles provides a fixed penal code for the navy; the army's temporary status historically justified different governance, though that distinction has diminished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges and post-service relief for sailors
rubrics_metrics.description: Sailors have similar relief provisions to soldiers (county rates, royal hospitals), rights to exercise trades after service, power to make informal testaments, and a higher threshold for arrest on debt (cannot be arrested unless debt sworn to be at least twenty pounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory protections recognize the public service of seamen and grant them particular civil privileges and protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law rejection of absolute slavery in England
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of England will not endure pure and proper slavery; the three classical grounds for slavery (captivity, voluntary sale of oneself, hereditary slavery) are rejected as inconsistent with natural law and reason. A slave or negro landing in England becomes a freeman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts or practices attempting to create absolute slavery are invalid in England; civil obligations (e.g., service contracts) remain enforceable but do not create a status of slavish property in person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Four main kinds identified: (1) menial servants (domestics), (2) apprentices (bound by indenture to learn trades), (3) labourers (hired by day or week, not intra moenia), and (4) superior/ministerial servants (stewards, factors, bailiffs) treated as servants pro tempore with respect to acts affecting master's property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different categories have different creation mechanisms, protections, and legal consequences (e.g., rights to wages, settlement, and scope of master's authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: General hiring construed as a year
rubrics_metrics.description: If hiring is general without specified time, the law construes it as a hiring for a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction rests on natural equity—servant serves and master maintains through seasonal revolutions; parties may contract for other terms expressly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion into service by justices and quarter's warning
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain persons (specified ages and situations) may be compelled by two justices to go out to service; neither master nor servant can terminate an unspecified hiring without a quarter's warning unless reasonable cause is allowed by a justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory mechanisms enforce labour availability and provide minimum notice protections for both parties; special bargains or mutual consent override these defaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship formation, capacity, and discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Apprentices bound by indenture for terms to be maintained and taught; statutes make minors capable of binding themselves; children of poor persons may be apprenticed by overseers with justice consent; apprentices may be discharged on reasonable cause with possible restitution of premium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apprenticeships are a statutory device to train trades; courts and sessions have equitable power to discharge and order restitution when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labourers' statutory regulation (Stat. 5 Eliz. c. 4.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute provides that persons with no visible means may be compelled to work, defines seasonal duration of work, punishes leaving/desertion, empowers justices/sheriff to settle wages, and penalizes paying or exacting wages different from settled rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute aims to regulate poor relief and labour markets, enforce local wage standards, and deter evasion or exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and exclusive trade rights from service/apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: Service (e.g., last service forty days) can give a settlement in a parish; apprentices have exclusive right to exercise their trade in England (statutory restriction only applies to trades in being at statute's making; village trades and seven years' actual service can suffice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apprenticeship confers both settlement and occupational privileges but subject to exceptions and judicial limitations; restrictions intended to ensure skill and employment of youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's limited right to correct servants
rubrics_metrics.description: A master may correct his apprentice or servant for negligence or misbehaviour provided it is done with moderation; if the master's wife beats a servant, that is good cause for departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law permits reasonable corporal correction but rejects abusive treatment; family members' violent acts can justify servant's leaving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal consequences for servants assaulting masters
rubrics_metrics.description: If any servant, workman, or labourer assaults his master or dame, he shall suffer one year's imprisonment and other open corporal punishment, not extending to life or limb (statutory provision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious penalties attach to assaults on employers, reflecting the gravity of breaching the master-servant relation by violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages entitlement and assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: By service all servants and labourers, except apprentices, become entitled to wages: menial servants according to agreement, labourers/husbandry servants according to sheriff or sessions appointment; statutes regulating wages apply to certain servants only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entitlement to wages is statutory/common-law based and varies by category of servant; magistrates may set rates where parties cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's right to maintain actions on behalf of servant and for loss of service
rubrics_metrics.description: A master may abet or assist his servant in actions at law (maintenance is generally an offence); master may bring action for beating or maiming his servant but must assign and prove his own damage by loss of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masters have proprietary interests in service that permit legal actions for interference or injury, but must demonstrate actual damage (loss of service).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual defence: master and servant may justify assaults in defence of each other
rubrics_metrics.description: A master may justify an assault in defence of his servant, and a servant in defence of his master; the master's interest in retaining service and the servant's duty of defence underpin this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive violence in protection of the master-servant relation may be legally justified under certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action for enticement or retention of servant
rubrics_metrics.description: If any person hires or retains another's servant and thereby the servant departs, the original master may have an action for damages against the new master and/or the servant (no action if new master ignorant of servitude unless refusal to restore after demand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law protects contractual service relations from improper interference by third parties, subject to notice/knowledge defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious liability for servant acts done by command
rubrics_metrics.description: If a servant commits a trespass by the command or encouragement of his master, the master is guilty; servants are not excused for obeying orders that are not honest and lawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master is liable for wrongful acts done pursuant to his directions; but servants remain personally responsible for obeying unlawful commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer liability for servants' habitual business acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts permitted in the usual course of a servant's business are equivalent to a general command (e.g., paying money to a banker's servant binds the banker; but if the servant's usual business does not include receiving money, the principal is not bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties can rely on the apparent authority created by customary business practice; distinctions depend on whether the act falls within the servant's customary duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's liability for servant negligence within service scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A master answers for damage negligently done by his servant while actually employed in the master's service (e.g., smith's servant laming a horse), but not for negligence occurring when servant is off duty; statute 6 Ann. c. 3 modifies common-law liability for accidental fires in houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope-of-employment is the key test for vicarious liability; statutory modifications may alter common-law remedies and penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master responsible for household nuisance
rubrics_metrics.description: A master is chargeable if any of his family cast or throw anything out of his house into the street causing individual damage or common nuisance; the master has superintendence of his household.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household control imposes responsibility for members' conduct creating public or private harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on profiting from one's own wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases, the master may be a loser by the trust reposed in his servant but cannot be a gainer; law disallows making advantage of one's own wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general equitable maxim prevents principals from benefiting from wrongful acts for which they (or their agents) are responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage treated as a civil contract
rubrics_metrics.description: The law regards marriage as a civil contract; its sanctity (holiness) is left to ecclesiastical law. For civil validity marriages require willingness, capacity to contract, and an actual contract in proper legal form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil courts address marriage's temporal effects and enforce contractual requisites; spiritual courts handle sin/consummation issues and can annul on canonical grounds for spiritual ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three requisites for a valid civil marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid marriage requires (1) willing consent of the parties ('consensus'), (2) legal capacity/ability to contract (no disqualifying disabilities), and (3) that the parties actually contracted in the forms and solemnities required by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil validity focuses on consent, capacity, and formal contracting; canonical impediments fall within ecclesiastical jurisdiction though they affect civil consequences if annulled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical impediments are voidable, not ipso facto void
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonical disabilities (e.g., pre-contract, consanguinity, affinity, some corporal infirmities) make a marriage voidable by the ecclesiastical courts but not automatically void at common law until sentence of nullity is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical impediments impact spiritual jurisdiction and may produce civil consequences only upon ecclesiastical determination; common law will treat such marriages as valid for civil purposes absent annulment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory limitation of degrees of impediment (32 Hen. VIII c. 38.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute 32 Hen. VIII c. 38 declares all marriages lawful except those prohibited by God's law and limits civil impediments to the Levitical degrees (up to uncle/niece). The statute also provided that consummated pre-contracts were treated as marriages, though some clauses have been repealed later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament curtailed ecclesiastical breadth of impediments to prevent abuses (e.g., buying off impediments) and to clarify civil effects; later statutes have modified these provisions.
